title: [portfolio] [M0][bd-BUG] Dolt dep-schema missing depends_on_id column (blocks all bd link)
description: bd dep add / bd link / --deps flag all fail with: Error 1105: column depends_on_id could not be found in any table in scope. Persists after: (1) bd init --force, (2) rm -rf .beads/embeddeddolt && bd bootstrap (which re-clones from remote). This means the corruption is in the remote Dolt schema, not just local. Impact: NO dependency edges can be wired for the entire portfolio-intel program, so bd ready cannot enforce phase/lane ordering. Workaround for now: rely on phase labels (m0/p0/p1/p2/p3/m4) + task titles for manual ordering. Real fix: file upstream to beads maintainers OR wait for bd binary upgrade with migration OR export-to-jsonl / drop-DB / bd init from scratch (would lose 83 items IDs). Reproducer: bd dep add OpenBBTechnical-qy83.2 --blocked-by OpenBBTechnical-qy83.1

description:

**Sites to fix (all P0 correctness):**

**Refactor scope:**

title: [QC-R1][correctness] openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/models/institutional_ownership.py:205 — Cache cleanup DELETEs all history per symbol before INSERT — writes destroy prior...
description:
## File
`openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/models/institutional_ownership.py:205`

## Finding
`_store_institutional` runs `DELETE FROM institutional_ownership WHERE symbol = %s` for every symbol in the batch, then inserts the fresh records. Because the FMP endpoint returns exactly ONE record per (symbol, year, quarter) and the cached fetcher is often called for a single specific quarter, this pattern wipes all previously cached quarters for that symbol on every write.

```python
cleanup_query = 'DELETE FROM institutional_ownership WHERE symbol = %s'
...
for symbol in symbols:
    execute_query(cleanup_query, (symbol,))

if params_list:
    execute_many(insert_query, params_list)
```

Effect: the cache never accumulates history. If a caller iterates `for q in 2020..2025: fetch(sym, year=y, quarter=q)`, each call deletes the previous quarter's cached row and inserts the new one, so on cold restart the cache holds exactly one period per symbol.

## Why this matters
Combined with finding #1 (cache doesn't respect year/quarter on read), this means the cache doesn't just fail to serve historical queries correctly — it *actively evicts* prior periods on every fetch. A time-series analytics workload gets zero cache benefit past the first query and gets a wrong-period return for subsequent queries in the TTL window. Also creates a race window: DELETE commits (autocommit connection), and any concurrent reader between DELETE and the INSERT sees zero rows.

## Suggested fix
Replace the DELETE + INSERT pattern with `INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` scoped to `(symbol, date, period)`. Add a UNIQUE index on `(symbol, date, period)` in `cache_schema.create_institutional_ownership_table` (currently only INDEX, not UNIQUE — see `openbb_fmp_cached/utils/cache_schema.py` line 4126-4132). This preserves prior quarters, avoids the race window, and eliminates the per-symbol DELETE queries (see performance finding #9).

## Category
`correctness`

## Confidence
87

## Priority override
0 (Refuter verdict: CONFIRMED — traced the FMP endpoint (openbb_fmp/models/institutional_ownership.py builds one URL per (symbol, year, quarter) and returns one summary row per URL). Skeptical scenario: is this actually a bulk endpoint that returns all quarters? No — the URL has explicit `year` and `quarter` querystring params, so it's period-specific. Data-loss finding upgraded to P0 (matches the existing balance_sheet.py pattern which has the same latent bug, so cross-repo fix).)

## Detected in
sweep 2026-07-03

title: [QC-R1][correctness] openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/models/institutional_ownership.py:176 — Cache read ignores year/quarter — returns wrong period for repeat callers
description:
## File
`openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/models/institutional_ownership.py:176`

## Finding
`_get_cached_institutional(symbol)` only filters by `symbol`, `is_valid`, and a 7-day `cached_at` cutoff — it does NOT filter by the caller's `query.year` / `query.quarter`. The step-1 loop in `aextract_data` (lines 77-84) similarly passes only the symbol, so a subsequent call for a different (year, quarter) will return whatever period happens to be sitting in the cache.

```python
def _get_cached_institutional(symbol: str) -> list[dict]:
    ...
    query = """
    SELECT data_json FROM institutional_ownership
    WHERE symbol = %s AND is_valid = TRUE AND cached_at >= %s
    ORDER BY date DESC
    """
```

Combined with finding #4 (the cleanup DELETE wipes prior history), the cache effectively acts as "remember the most recent single request" — and then returns it verbatim for every query in the next 7 days regardless of the year/quarter asked for.

## Why this matters
A caller that scans historical quarters (e.g. `for q in 2020..2025: obb.equity.ownership.institutional(sym, year=y, quarter=q)`) will get the first quarter's data returned for every subsequent quarter query within the TTL window. This silently poisons any historical / time-series analytics built on this endpoint, without any log warning and without any test coverage for the mismatch.

## Suggested fix
Include `year` and `quarter` in the cache key. Either (a) add `year` and `quarter` columns to the `institutional_ownership` table and filter on them in `_get_cached_institutional`, or (b) encode `(symbol, year, quarter)` into a composite lookup key stored in a dedicated column. Also pass `query` into `_get_cached_institutional` so the filter can be applied. The `aextract_data` step-1 loop must be updated to pass those values.

## Priority override

Refuter verdict: CONFIRMED — the base `FMPInstitutionalOwnershipFetcher.aextract_data` explicitly builds URLs with `year` and `quarter` in the querystring (fmp/institutional_ownership.py line 200-203), proving the endpoint is period-specific and cache-by-symbol-only is incorrect.)

## Finding
Two of the 66 create-table functions build DDL by f-string interpolation of a Python-computed table name:

```python
def create_analyst_estimates_table():
    table_name = get_table_name("analyst_estimates")

    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS {table_name} (
```

Today `get_table_name` only prepends `test_` to a hard-coded literal, so no user input reaches the DDL string and this is not exploitable. But the pattern is one refactor away from injection: the moment anyone thinks 'let's allow the table prefix to come from an env var / config / user setting', the interpolation becomes a SQL identifier injection vector (MySQL doesn't support parameterized identifiers, so f-strings will look like the natural fix).

Secondary concern: `execute_query(query)` at line 102 passes an empty `params=()` — so this DDL runs unparameterized. If a caller ever passes literal data through the same pathway, they'll do it the same way.

Not exploitable today, but a fragile-by-construction pattern in a security-relevant place (DDL). Once the two examples exist, the next contributor sees them as the template.

## Suggested fix
Whitelist-validate `base_name` inside `get_table_name` — `assert re.match(r'^[a-z_][a-z0-9_]*$', base_name)`. Or better, restrict the allowed set to `FLATTENED_TABLES.keys()`. That way the invariant is enforced structurally rather than by hoping future callers behave.

title: [QC-R1][security] openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/utils/database.py:241 — init_database uses f-string interpolation for CREATE DATABASE with unvalidated database_name
description:
## File

## Finding
```python
cursor.execute(f"CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS {database_name}")
```

`database_name` originates from `mysql_database` / `db_database` / `database_name` in `user_settings.json`, or the `DB_NAME` environment variable (see `_load_config`), or the hardcoded default. There is no validation that the string is a valid MySQL identifier -- no character-set check, no length check, no escape/quote. A configuration like `mysql_database: 'foo; DROP DATABASE prod; --'` would execute two statements.

Parameterized queries (`%s`) cannot be used for DDL identifiers, so this specifically requires an identifier-quoting helper.

## Why this matters
The attacker model is narrow (must control user_settings.json or env vars, at which point they already have process access), but the pattern is still a code-review flag: DDL with string interpolation is the same class of bug that appears in higher-impact contexts (multi-tenant SaaS). Static analyzers (bandit, semgrep) will flag this. It also fails safe design: even trusted local config should not be silently trusted to be well-formed.

## Suggested fix
Validate `database_name` against a regex (e.g. `^[A-Za-z0-9_]{1,64}$`) before interpolating, and raise a clear `ValueError` otherwise. Wrap with backticks: `CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS \`{database_name}\`` -- but backticks alone don't defend against embedded backticks; the regex check is the real defense.

title: [QC-R1][security] openbb_platform/extensions/techtrade/openbb_techtrade/reporting/excel_export.py:296 — User-controlled export path allows arbitrary filesystem writes (path traversal)
description:

## Finding
`ExportConfig.path: str | None` is a free-form string forwarded through the REST-facing router `export_router.export()` (POST /techtrade/export). The exporter calls `Path(cfg.path)` (line 781), `path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` (line 782), and `workbook.save(path)` (line 657) with no whitelist, no repo-root containment check, no basename sanitization, and no rejection of absolute paths or `..` segments. ## Why this matters
When this router is served behind a REST endpoint (or any tenant boundary), user-supplied paths become an arbitrary-write primitive: overwriting arbitrary xlsx targets, creating deep directory trees to fill inodes, or triggering side effects in watched folders. The mitigation the code appears to intend — the `TECHTRADE_EXPORT_DIR` env default — only applies when `path is None`; an explicit `path=` argument bypasses it entirely.

## Suggested fix
In `export()` (or in the router wrapper), resolve `cfg.path` against a configured base dir and reject any resolution that escapes it: `resolved = (base_dir / cfg.path).resolve(); resolved.relative_to(base_dir.resolve())` (raises ValueError on escape). title: [QC-R1][security] openbb_platform/extensions/backtest/openbb_backtest/analytics/export.py:87 — Path traversal via unvalidated `name` in _resolve_export_path allows writing anywhere
description:
## File
`openbb_platform/extensions/backtest/openbb_backtest/analytics/export.py:87`

## Finding
`_resolve_export_path(name, export_dir, timestamp)` returns `Path(export_dir) / f"{stem}.html"` where `stem` is derived directly from the caller-supplied `name` (only `.html` suffix stripping is performed). Python's `Path` __truediv__ does no normalization: `Path('Analysis/exports') / '../../etc/passwd'` yields `Analysis/exports/../../etc/passwd`, and if the right side is *absolute* (e.g. `/etc/passwd` or `C:\Windows\Temp\evil`) it discards the left side entirely. `export_html` then calls `out_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` and hands the fully unresolved path to `quantstats.reports.html(..., output=str(out_path), ...)`, so an attacker (or a buggy upstream caller) who controls `name` can create arbitrary directories and overwrite any file the process can write.

```python
# line 95
if name:
    stem = name[:-5] if name.endswith('.html') else name  # accepts '../../evil' or '/abs/path'
# line 100
return Path(export_dir) / f"{stem}.html"
```

## Why this matters
(agent did not provide a separate why_it_matters — see description above)

## Suggested fix
Reject or sanitize path separators and absolute paths before building the output path. Minimal fix:
```python
from pathlib import PurePath
if name:
    candidate = PurePath(name)
    if candidate.is_absolute() or '..' in candidate.parts or any(sep in name for sep in ('/', '\\')):
        raise ValueError(f'name must be a plain file stem, got: {name!r}')
    stem = name[:-5] if name.endswith('.html') else name
```
Alternatively, resolve the final path and assert it lives under the resolved `export_dir` (containment check). Add a unit test covering `name='../foo'`, `name='/tmp/foo'`, and (Windows) `name='C:\\foo'`.

title: [QC-R1][security] Tools/parse_fidelity_positions.py:1224 — f-string SQL for CREATE DATABASE with unvalidated --database CLI value permits identifier injection
description:
## File
`Tools/parse_fidelity_positions.py:1224`

## Finding
`get_connection` accepts a `database` name from the CLI (`--database`) and interpolates it directly into a `CREATE DATABASE` DDL statement using an f-string:

```python
def get_connection(database: Optional[str] = None):
    ...
    if database:
        params["database"] = database
    db_name = params.pop("database")
    conn = pymysql.connect(**params)
    try:
        with conn.cursor() as cur:
            cur.execute(f"CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS `{db_name}`")   # <-- interpolated
```

MySQL DDL cannot use parameter binding for identifiers, so an f-string is unavoidable — but there is no validation of `db_name`. A value like `foo`; DROP DATABASE bar; --` breaks out of the backticks and executes arbitrary DDL. In a script that gets pasted into shell one-liners or invoked from ops tooling this is a genuine injection surface.

## Why this matters
Even though this is a local script, `--database` can be forwarded from higher-level scripts or CI pipelines. The interpolation runs as whatever user the MySQL account represents, and that user has CREATE DATABASE privilege. There's no allowlist, no length cap, no character check.

## Suggested fix
Validate against a strict pattern before interpolation and reject anything else:

```python
import re
if not re.fullmatch(r"[A-Za-z0-9_]{1,64}", db_name):
    raise ValueError(f"Invalid database name: {db_name!r}")
cur.execute(f"CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS `{db_name}`")
```

title: [QC-R1][correctness] Tools/parse_fidelity_positions.py:1224 — autocommit=True + DELETE-then-INSERT loop risks losing prior snapshot on partial failure
description:
## File
`Tools/parse_fidelity_positions.py:1224`

## Finding
`get_connection` unconditionally returns a connection with `autocommit=True`, and both `persist_to_mysql` and `persist_basket_positions_to_mysql` use the pattern DELETE-all-rows-for-this-snapshot then INSERT-row-by-row in an `iterrows()` loop:

```python
# get_connection
return pymysql.connect(**params, cursorclass=pymysql.cursors.DictCursor, autocommit=True)

# persist_to_mysql
cur.execute("DELETE FROM Portfolio_Positions WHERE snapshot_date = %s", (snap_val,))  # COMMITTED IMMEDIATELY
for _, row in df.iterrows():
    cur.execute(INSERT_SQL, (...))                                                       # ANY FAILURE HERE = DATA LOSS
```

With autocommit, the DELETE is durable before the INSERTs run. If a single row raises (bad type, disconnect, integer overflow, transient network error), the prior snapshot is gone and the new one is partial.

## Why this matters
This is destructive persistence of financial positions with no rollback path. A single malformed lot (unexpected currency string, oversized VARCHAR, MySQL restart mid-loop) permanently erases the previous good snapshot and leaves the table in a half-imported state. There's no `--dry-run` protection here either — this is the default path. The whole point of the delete-then-insert idempotency strategy assumes atomicity that autocommit destroys.

## Suggested fix
Remove `autocommit=True` from `get_connection` (or make it opt-in), wrap each `persist_*` operation in an explicit transaction, and commit only after the INSERT loop succeeds:

```python
conn = get_connection(database)  # autocommit=False
try:
    with conn.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute("DELETE ...", ...)
        cur.executemany(INSERT_SQL, rows_as_tuples)
        _rebuild_portfolio_basket_for_snapshot(cur, snap_val)
    conn.commit()
except Exception:
    conn.rollback()
    raise
finally:
    conn.close()
```

## Category
`correctness`

## Confidence
95

## Priority override
0 (Data-loss risk on the main persistence path for financial data with no rollback and no dry-run guard on the destructive branch.)

## Refuter verdict
**Verdict:** `confirmed` (confidence 80)

The technical bug is real and I could not construct a strong recovery path that removes the underlying data-loss window. Verified findings:

1) Call chain confirmed. persist_to_mysql (line 1268) calls conn = get_connection(database). get_connection (lines 1224-1247) returns pymysql.connect(..., cursorclass=DictCursor, autocommit=True). Same connection is used for the DELETE (lines 1305-1308) and the row-by-row INSERT loop (lines 1316-1340). No secondary connection or context manager overrides autocommit.

2) autocommit=True semantics are as described. Per pymysql, autocommit=True issues SET autocommit=1 on the session so every statement is committed as soon as MySQL executes it. The DELETE is durable on disk before the first INSERT runs. Since the loop is not wrapped in START TRANSACTION / conn.begin(), each INSERT is also its own auto-committed transaction — an exception mid-loop leaves prior INSERTs committed and later ones missing, with the pre-existing snapshot already gone.

3) No rollback path. The try (line 1269) has only a finally: conn.close() (line 1365). There is no except that would attempt recovery, and even if there were, conn.rollback() is a no-op after a committed statement. There is no shadow / audit / backup table (only Portfolio_Positions, Account_Owner, portfolio_basket are created; none of them mirror rows for rollback).

4) No upsert strategy. INSERT_SQL (line 688) is a plain INSERT — no ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, no REPLACE INTO. Portfolio_Positions has AUTO_INCREMENT PK plus indexes on snapshot_date and (account_name, basket_name), but no unique key that would let an upsert replace rows in place. DELETE-then-INSERT is the only implemented idempotency mechanism.

5) --dry-run exists but only gates the whole persist_to_mysql call at line 1770; there is no --dry-run guard inside persist_to_mysql itself, so once the caller enters the function the DELETE will run against the live table.

Mitigations considered (and why they don't fully rescue the finding):
- Recovery from source HTML: the docstring (line 1259-1261) explicitly says re-imports of the same HTML are idempotent, and snapshot_date is derived from the 'As of' timestamp in the HTML, so a user who still has the .html on disk can re-run and restore the snapshot. This is a genuine mitigation and is why I did not raise confidence higher.
- Scope of loss: DELETE is scoped to WHERE snapshot_date = %s (or additionally AND account_name IN (...) with --merge_snapshot at lines 1295-1302), so historical snapshots with different dates are untouched. The blast radius is one snapshot_date (or one snapshot_date × account set in merge mode).
- Interactive CLI: users typically run this manually and would notice the traceback, prompting a re-run.

Even with those mitigations, the recovery path depends on the operator (a) still having the exact source HTML file, (b) noticing the failure, and (c) knowing to re-run. In a financial pipeline that is not a strong recovery path — HTML exports are manual downloads that get cleaned up, cron jobs mask exceptions, and a half-populated Portfolio_Positions with the same snapshot_date is easy to mistake for a completed import (row count is >0). Per the reviewer guidance, data-loss risks in financial pipelines are worth filing at high severity even if recoverable.

P0 override assessment: I think the P0 override is aggressive but defensible. The fix is trivial (wrap DELETE+INSERTs in a single transaction: pass autocommit=False and add conn.commit() at the end of the `with conn.cursor()` block, or issue START TRANSACTION and COMMIT explicitly), and until fixed there is a real window where the table can be observed as partial or empty for the affected snapshot_date. I'd support keeping it as P0 or downgrading to P1/High — either is defensible, but the finding itself is not a false positive.

close_reason: shipped in PR #422 (merged eb06442) — Tools/parse_fidelity_positions.py get_connection now defaults autocommit=False; 3 persist functions (persist_to_mysql, persist_basket_positions_to_mysql, persist_basket_intended_weight_csv) wrapped in try/commit/except/rollback/finally. 10 unit tests + 1 review-fix commit addressing code-reviewer P0 (missed 3rd caller) + P1 (weak magic-number assertion). `url = f"{FMP_STABLE}/profile?symbol={symbol}&apikey={api_key}"` (line 173). Lines 121-127 build the git argv as `['git', 'clone', ..., url, str(local)]` and `['git', '-C', str(local), 'pull', '--ff-only']`. Insert `--` before positional arguments: `cmd += ['--', url, str(local)]` for clone, and validate/normalise `target` (reject paths starting with `-`, or `abspath(target)` before use) at `resolve_target`.

title: [QC-R1][security] openbb_platform/extensions/agents/openbb_agents/mcp_server.py:110 — Auto-discovery exposes any new public function in portfolio_tools as an LLM-callable tool with no whitelist
description:
## File
`openbb_platform/extensions/agents/openbb_agents/mcp_server.py:110`

## Finding
`collect_tools` walks every public function in `_TOOL_MODULES` and registers each as an MCP tool:

```python
for module in _TOOL_MODULES:
    for name, fn in inspect.getmembers(module, inspect.isfunction):
        if name.startswith("_") or name in seen:
            continue
        ...
        tools.append({...})
```

There is no explicit allow-list. The capability boundary is `startswith("_")` — a single-character naming mistake (`def cancel_order(...)` instead of `def _cancel_order(...)`) silently promotes a function into the LLM's tool set. There is no per-tool review gate, no `@mcp_expose` decorator, and no runtime schema showing which capabilities the LLM has.

## Why this matters
MCP tool capabilities are the trust boundary between the LLM and the user's account/data. Auto-discovery inverts the safe default: 'private unless marked public' becomes 'public unless someone remembers the underscore'. When portfolio_tools grows to include mutating operations (place order, close position, transfer funds), this pattern will silently expose them.

## Suggested fix
Require an explicit opt-in decorator, e.g.:

```python
def mcp_tool(fn):
    fn.__mcp_exposed__ = True
    return fn

# in collect_tools:
if not getattr(fn, "__mcp_exposed__", False):
    continue
```

Or maintain an explicit `_EXPOSED_TOOLS: set[str]` in the tool module and only register names in that set. Log the final registered tool list at startup so drift is visible.

## Confidence
80

title: [QC-R1][security] openbb_platform/extensions/agents/openbb_agents/mcp_server.py:166 — Exception messages returned to LLM via json.dumps(default=str) may leak paths/secrets/internal state
description:
## File
`openbb_platform/extensions/agents/openbb_agents/mcp_server.py:166`

## Finding
In `call_tool`, on any tool exception the raw `str(exc)` is serialized back to the LLM client:

```python
except Exception as exc:
    logger.error("Tool %r raised: %s", name, exc, exc_info=True)
    return [TextContent(type="text", text=json.dumps({"error": str(exc)}))]
```

Exceptions raised deeper in the tool layer (e.g. `openbb.equity.profile` provider failures, filesystem errors from `data.get_portfolio_basket_df`, SQL errors) commonly embed absolute file paths, credential fragments, DSN strings, cache directory paths, or HTTP URLs with query params. All of these become directly visible to the LLM (and thus to a malicious prompt-injection payload that then exfiltrates them).

## Why this matters
MCP servers are an untrusted-model boundary. A single credential fragment or absolute path in an exception message reaching the LLM turns into whatever the LLM's downstream sink is — chat log, upstream training data, follow-up tool call to a webhook. This is the classic MCP info-disclosure pattern.

## Suggested fix
Return a generic error string and only log the detailed message locally. E.g.:

```python
except Exception as exc:
    logger.error("Tool %r raised", name, exc_info=True)
    return [TextContent(type="text", text=json.dumps({
        "error": "tool_failed",
        "tool": name,
    }))]
```

Optionally include a redacted / classified error kind (`ValueError`, `TimeoutError`, `AuthError`) but never `str(exc)` verbatim.

title: [QC-R1][provider-contract] openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/models/institutional_ownership.py:361 — Unbounded parallel yfinance calls in `_try_yfinance` — no concurrency cap o...
description:
## File
`openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/models/institutional_ownership.py:361`

## Finding
`_try_yfinance` builds `tasks = [_get_one(sym) for sym in symbols]` and calls `asyncio.gather(*tasks)` with no concurrency cap:

```python
tasks = [_get_one(sym) for sym in symbols]
fetched = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
```

A caller passing `symbol='AAPL,MSFT,GOOG,...'` with N symbols spawns N concurrent yfinance HTTP calls (each `_get_one` does at least two calls — `get_info` and `get_major_holders`). Yahoo Finance has no published rate limit but is known to 429 and IP-ban aggressive scrapers. For screening use cases (100+ symbols), this fires 200+ concurrent requests.

## Why this matters
IP bans from Yahoo affect every yfinance-backed OpenBB installation sharing an egress IP (CI, shared workspaces). Because yfinance is the free-tier fallback for users without an FMP paid plan, this path is on the hot path for the majority of installations.

## Suggested fix
Bound concurrency with a semaphore, e.g. `sem = asyncio.Semaphore(5)` and wrap `_get_one` in `async with sem:`. Also consider adding a small jitter between calls if the semaphore isn't enough. The `openbb_yfinance` provider itself may already have batching helpers — check `openbb_yfinance/utils/references.py` for reusable primitives before rolling a local semaphore.

title: [QC-R1][correctness] openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/models/institutional_ownership.py:119 — `transform_data` silently drops schema-invalid records at debug level
description:
## File
`openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/models/institutional_ownership.py:119`

## Finding
`transform_data` wraps `FMPInstitutionalOwnershipData.model_validate(record)` in a bare `except Exception:` and logs at `logger.debug` — meaning any record that fails validation is silently dropped without a user-visible warning.

```python
for record in data:
    try:
        validated.append(FMPInstitutionalOwnershipData.model_validate(record))
    except Exception:
        logger.debug('Skipping record that does not match FMP schema: %s',
                     record.get('symbol', 'unknown'))
```

The intent (per the docstring on line 125) is to "tolerate missing fields from fallback sources." But because both fallback sources (yfinance in `_try_yfinance` and SEC 13F in `_try_sec_13f`) already build records with every FMP-required field populated with 0/0.0 defaults, this except-and-drop path should never fire in practice. If it does fire, it's masking a real schema drift — and debug-level logging is invisible under the default logging config.

## Why this matters
If the FMP schema changes (e.g. a required field is renamed) or a fallback source returns a malformed record, the caller sees an empty result with no signal about why. That's the exact silent-failure pattern the OpenBB CLAUDE.md and the pr-review-toolkit's silent-failure-hunter agent are meant to catch. Users end up debugging "why is institutional ownership empty for AAPL?" with no log evidence.

## Suggested fix
Log at `logger.warning` with the specific validation error: `logger.warning('Dropping institutional-ownership record for %s due to schema mismatch: %s', symbol, exc)`. Consider raising an aggregate exception if *all* records fail validation (the fallback design assumes at least one succeeds — a complete drop is a bug, not a tolerable state).

title: [QC-R1][correctness] openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/models/institutional_ownership.py:317 — yfinance fallback stores snapshot data with `date=today` — semantic mismatch with...
description:
## File
`openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/models/institutional_ownership.py:317`

## Finding
The yfinance path builds a record with `date: today.isoformat()`, but the fields it populates (`investors_holding`, `ownership_percent`) come from yfinance's `Ticker.info` — which reflects the *current snapshot* aggregated across the latest available filings, not a specific quarter.

```python
today = date.today()
return {
    'symbol': symbol.upper(),
    'cik': None,
    'date': today.isoformat(),
    'investors_holding': info.get('institutionsCount', 0) or 0,
    ...
}
```

Storing this record in a table keyed on a quarterly-summary schema means the cache now contains rows whose `date` is (say) `2026-07-03` but whose `period` is unstated, alongside rows from FMP with `date` = quarter-end. Downstream queries that `ORDER BY date DESC` will always return the yfinance snapshot before any legitimate quarterly record.

## Why this matters
The FMP contract is quarterly summary. Mixing a rolling snapshot into the same table (a) breaks the `ORDER BY date DESC` semantics of `_get_cached_institutional`, (b) makes it impossible for downstream analytics to distinguish snapshot vs quarterly source without introspecting `data_source`, and (c) combined with finding #4 (cleanup wipes all history), a single yfinance-fallback call permanently poisons the cache for that symbol.

## Suggested fix
Either (a) do not persist yfinance snapshots to the shared `institutional_ownership` cache — keep them in a separate `institutional_ownership_snapshot` table with different semantics; or (b) set `date` to the most recent quarter-end that has *definitely* been reported (period_end + 45 days ago) rather than `today()`; or (c) at minimum populate a `period` field and require callers to filter by it.

title: [QC-R1][correctness] openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/models/institutional_ownership.py:431 — SEC 13F fallback uses period-end as `date` — PIT look-ahead (45-day filing lag ig...
description:
## File
`openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/models/institutional_ownership.py:431`

## Finding
In `_try_sec_13f`, the record's `date` field is set to `_period_to_date(period).isoformat()`, which is the quarter-end date (e.g. `2024-12-31` for `'2024-Q4'`). But 13F filings have a **45-day statutory lag** — filings for Q4 2024 are not required to be filed until February 14, 2025. The code emits a record whose `date` field claims the data existed on the quarter-end date, when in reality it was not filed (and therefore not knowable) until up to 45 days later.

```python
period = holders[0].get('period')
...
as_of = _period_to_date(period)
results.append({
    'symbol': symbol.upper(),
    'date': as_of.isoformat(),   # <-- period end, not filing date
    ...
})
```

The FMP standard model documents `date` as the "reporting date," so this is arguably schema-compliant — but downstream code in `Analysis/` that treats `date` as the availability date for point-in-time analysis will silently look ahead 45 days.

## Why this matters
For any backtest or PIT-safe screener that uses `date` as "when this data became knowable" (a natural reading), this fallback path introduces a 45-day look-ahead bias per record. The bias is consistent with the base FMP model contract, but the FMP model at least has the excuse that the FMP API only serves records after they've been filed — the SEC 13F fallback is populated from a locally-ingested index that may contain records the moment the ingestor picks them up, without any 45-day availability guarantee.

## Suggested fix
Either (a) add a `filing_date` / `available_date` field to the record equal to `period_end + timedelta(days=45)` (or the actual filing date if the 13F index tracks it), and require downstream PIT code to filter on that field; or (b) shift `date` itself to the availability date and document the deviation from the base FMP contract; or (c) at minimum add a warning in the docstring flagging the PIT hazard for downstream consumers. Also worth cross-checking the yfinance path (line 321), which uses `date.today()` — that has its own semantic mismatch with the quarterly-summary contract (see finding #6).

## Category
`correctness`

## Confidence
85

## Priority override
1 (Refuter verdict: CONFIRMED WITH CAVEAT — the FMP standard model does define `date` as the reporting period end, so the fallback is contract-consistent. The finding is really about the downstream PIT hazard rather than the fallback per se. That said, this file *chose* to populate `date` from `period` when it could have used filing_date, so a comment/warning is warranted here at the source of the ambiguity. In `_try_yfinance`, multiply `inst_pct` by 100 before storing, so the value enters the model in FMP's percent form and the validator normalizes it back to the fraction: `"ownership_percent": inst_pct * 100 if inst_pct is not None else 0.0`. ## File

## Finding
The module uses seven `except Exception:` blocks (lines 58, 133, 145, 154, 192, 201, 260, plus the bare `except Exception:` at 212 in `_is_cache_sufficient`), all with `logger.warning(...)` (or silent) recovery. None call `logger.exception(...)`, so tracebacks are never emitted — only the `str(exc)` message.

Consequences:

1. A `TypeError` from a signature change in `repository.read_cached_rows` (a programmer bug) is caught at line 192, logged as `"Complementary cache read failed: read_cached_rows() takes 3 positional arguments but 4 were given"` — reader assumes cache is down, misses the code bug.

In `_fetch_with_fallback`, catching all `Exception` on lines 133, 145, 154 means an `asyncio.CancelledError` (which is a `BaseException` in 3.8+, so actually _not_ caught — good) is fine, but a `MemoryError`, `RecursionError`, or `ImportError` from a broken source adapter is silently classified as "upstream_failure" and drifts through the fallback chain.

Combined with the lack of `logger.exception`, root-causing any of these is a code-diving exercise; there is no traceback in logs.

## Why this matters
Silent-failure amplifier: every upstream outage, every code bug in the sources module, every DB schema drift shows up as the same generic WARNING with a message string. Operators can't triage. Tests don't catch the code-bug case because the tests mock the repository. This is exactly the class of finding the QC sweep exists to catch — the module _looks_ defensive but is actually swallowing signal.

## Suggested fix
For all cache-read/write and source-fetch handlers, use `logger.exception("...")` instead of `logger.warning("...: %s", exc)` — `exception()` includes the full traceback at WARNING level in the emitted record. title: [QC-R1][correctness] openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/complementary/free_yield_service.py:61 — `freshness_cutoff` is naive local-time `datetime.now()` compared against DB `CUR...
description:
## File
`openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/complementary/free_yield_service.py:61`

## Finding
Line 61: `freshness_cutoff = datetime.now() - timedelta(hours=ttl_hours)` — naive datetime in the process's local timezone.

Cache writes (repository.py:53-54) use SQL `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`, which in MySQL/MariaDB is evaluated in the DB server's session TZ (usually UTC in containerized deployments, but this is configurable per-connection). The SQL SELECT (repository.py:33) compares:

```sql
AND cached_at >= %s
```

where `%s` is bound as the client's naive local `datetime.now() - ttl`. If the client runs in UTC+9 (Tokyo) and the DB stores timestamps in UTC, the client's `datetime.now()` is 9 hours _ahead_ of what the DB thinks is "now". So `freshness_cutoff` (bound naive) is compared to `cached_at` (stored in DB's UTC) as if they're the same timezone. A row cached 5 hours ago (11 in DB clock) is compared to a cutoff of 15 (24-9) — the row is (wrongly) treated as expired 9 hours early.

Same drift the other way for negative offsets: cache treated as fresh for `ttl_hours + offset` hours instead of `ttl_hours`.

`datetime.utcnow()` is used elsewhere in `repository.py:73` for `retrieved_at`, indicating awareness of TZ concerns — but this one gap defeats the design.

## Why this matters
For non-UTC client deployments, cache freshness is systematically wrong by the process TZ offset. Users in Asia/Europe get cache re-fetched hours earlier than intended (more FMP calls; the exact thing the module tries to avoid). Worse, users west of UTC (US Pacific) get stale data served past its intended expiry. Both fail-modes silent — there is no log or alert, and the unit tests all mock the repository so this never trips in CI.

## Suggested fix
Replace with `datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(hours=ttl_hours)` (aware datetime). If the underlying DB driver strips tzinfo before binding, either (a) explicitly set the DB session TZ to UTC in `init_database()` and compute cutoffs in UTC-naive form, or (b) store `cached_at` as an explicit UTC ISO string / BIGINT epoch and compare in that space. Either way, drop the naive `datetime.now()` from the freshness math.

## File
`openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/complementary/free_yield_service.py:205`

## Finding
Sufficiency test:

```python
return min(row_dates) <= start and max(row_dates) >= end
```

US10Y (`^TNX` / DGS10 / FMP treasury) is bond-market data — no weekend rows, no US-holiday rows. If `_normalize_dates` defaults `end` to `datetime.now().date()` and the caller invokes the service on any Saturday, Sunday, or bank holiday, the cache will contain data up to the prior trading day (say Friday). `max(row_dates) = Friday < end = Saturday`, so the check returns `False`, and the full fallback pipeline (FMP → FRED → Yahoo) runs on every call — the entire weekend and every holiday.

The cache TTL layer (`freshness_cutoff` at line 61) also doesn't rescue this: the freshness gate is applied _inside_ `read_cached_rows` (`AND cached_at >= %s`), so if the cache is fresh but incomplete-by-this-test's definition, it's still skipped. The result is that a well-populated cache is wasted every non-trading day.

## Why this matters
This turns a cache-first design into a fetch-first design for ~30% of the calendar (weekends + ~10 US holidays a year). Given the whole `complementary` module exists specifically so the free-tier FMP call limit isn't exhausted, this is a self-defeating bug — the cache thrashes exactly on the days when reducing outbound calls matters most (batch backtests over weekends, off-hours agent workflows). For a heavy consumer, this may accelerate FMP rate-limit exhaustion by an order of magnitude.

## Suggested fix
Change the sufficiency contract to "cache covers the range up to the last _expected trading day_ on or before `end`". Simplest implementation: replace the `>= end` check with `>= min(end, _last_trading_day(end))`. A cheap approximation (no calendar dep) is `_last_trading_day = end` shifted back to Mon-Fri, tolerating US holidays as an acceptable false-positive re-fetch (worst case ~10 refetches/year). If the `pandas_market_calendars` dependency is acceptable, use `mcal.get_calendar("NYSE").schedule(...)` for exact answers.

title: [QC-R1][correctness] openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/complementary/free_yield_service.py:126 — FMP retry loop has no backoff, only exception-triggered (not empty-data-trigger...
description:
## File
`openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/complementary/free_yield_service.py:126`

## Finding
Three tightly-coupled defects in the retry block:

```python
MAX_FMP_RETRIES = 2   # line 20

for attempt in range(1, MAX_FMP_RETRIES + 1):   # line 128 → attempts=1,2
    try:
        rows = await fmp_source.fetch_us10y(start_date, end_date, credentials, **kwargs)
        if rows:
            return rows
    except Exception as exc:
        last_exception = exc
        if attempt < MAX_FMP_RETRIES:
            continue
```

1. **Naming**: `MAX_FMP_RETRIES = 2` reads as "two retries after the initial call = three total calls". Actually `range(1, 3)` yields two iterations → one initial call + one retry only.
2. **No backoff**: `continue` fires immediately with no `await asyncio.sleep(...)`. Two back-to-back FMP calls collide with the exact rate-limiter that failed the first call — the retry has near-zero recovery value for HTTP 429 or transient throttling.
3. **Empty-data path never retries**: when `fmp_source.fetch_us10y` returns `[]` (no rows, e.g., FMP starter-tier returns empty for treasury endpoints — see `_classify_fmp_failure` explicitly labelling this `"empty_data"` at line 270), the loop falls through the `if rows: return rows` block without retrying. Yet the whole fallback-to-FRED transition is logged with trigger `"empty_data"` (line 138-139), suggesting the intent was to treat empty as retryable.

Also: the loop exits without incrementing `last_exception` on the empty path, so the FMP-to-FRED transition log shows `trigger="empty_data"` (from `_classify_fmp_failure(None)`), which is at least internally consistent — but the exception classification path for a 429 rate limit produces `"transient_after_retries"` (line 277) after only one retry, which reads as "we tried hard" when we tried once.

## Why this matters
Under FMP throttling (a common condition given this is the free-tier cache provider), the code fails through to FRED after ~2 HTTP calls in ~1 second. FRED has its own throttling and may also fail. The effective retry budget is much smaller than the code reads. Combined with no async backoff, a burst of concurrent `get_us10y_series` callers will slam FMP simultaneously, guarantee 429s, and cascade-degrade to Yahoo (the sync-blocking branch above). The constant name misleads any future maintainer trying to raise the retry budget.

## Suggested fix
Rename to `MAX_FMP_ATTEMPTS = 2`. Add `await asyncio.sleep(2 ** (attempt - 1) * 0.5)` in the `continue` branch (500ms, 1s). If empty rows should be retried, move the empty-check into the `else` clause and set `last_exception = None` when the last attempt still returned empty. Document the semantics in a comment.

description:
## File

## Finding
Every table declares both:

```sql
data_json JSON DEFAULT NULL,
additional_fields JSON DEFAULT NULL,
```

There is no docstring, comment, or code-level convention documenting the split. In practice both columns can be `NULL`, both can hold overlapping keys, and downstream reads have no way to know which is authoritative when they diverge. The kitchen-sink flat columns (`market_cap`, `eps`, ...) are a third potentially-authoritative source for the same values.

This is a three-way merge problem for every read: which of `flat_col`, `data_json['field']`, `additional_fields['field']` is right?

When the three sources disagree — e.g., because a partial re-fetch updated the flat column but not the JSON — silent data inconsistency shows up in downstream analytics with no way to detect which value is the vendor's actual answer. In an audit or debugging session, no one can tell what the 'true' cache state is.

Pick one authoritative representation: either (a) drop the flat columns and store only the JSON blob (with a well-defined JSON schema per table), or (b) drop `data_json` and only extract into typed flat columns. If both must coexist, at minimum drop `additional_fields` (redundant with `data_json`) and add a module-level comment stating the invariant `flat_column ≡ data_json[column_name] when both non-NULL; on divergence, flat_column is authoritative`. Then add a test that verifies this on every read path.

title: [QC-R1][provider-contract] openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/utils/cache_schema.py:86 — No point-in-time (PIT) columns — restated financials silently overwrite history
description:
## File
`openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/utils/cache_schema.py:86`

## Finding
Every table has `cached_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` and `is_valid BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE` (line 86-87 and repeated). No table has:

- `as_of_date` / `effective_date` — the vendor's stated PIT for the row
- `ingested_at` — separate from `cached_at`, records the *first* time we saw this exact tuple (so we can distinguish 'the value we saw first' from 'the current cached value')
- `restatement_flag` / `revision_number` — companies restate income statements; without a version column, revision N silently overwrites revision N-1 and the original figures are lost forever

`cached_at` alone captures 'when this row landed in our cache', which is not the same as 'when the vendor said this was true' — the two diverge whenever a filing is revised or a historical adjustment is backdated.

## Why this matters
OpenBB's positioning is 'connect once, consume everywhere' — for financial analytics that specifically means users expect a fixed answer to 'what did MSFT's 2019 EPS look like on 2020-01-01' (before subsequent restatements). This schema cannot answer that question — the current value is the only value stored, and any historical backtest that depends on point-in-time correctness will be silently wrong. This is a foundational design issue and is a `provider-contract` finding rather than a garden-variety bug.

## Suggested fix
Add `as_of_date DATE NOT NULL` and `ingested_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP NOT NULL` to every fact table, and shift the UNIQUE key to `(symbol, date, period, as_of_date)`. Update the loader to insert a new row (not update in place) when the same `(symbol, date, period)` tuple returns a different value on a subsequent pull. Readers that want 'latest' pick the max `ingested_at`; PIT backtests filter `ingested_at <= <backtest-date>`. If this is out of scope for a cache-only layer, at minimum document in a module docstring that this cache is NOT PIT-safe so callers don't accidentally use it for backtests.

title: [QC-R1][correctness] openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/utils/cache_schema.py:5469 — create_all_flattened_tables silently swallows DDL failures and continues
description:
## File
`openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/utils/cache_schema.py:5469`

## Finding
```python
def create_all_flattened_tables():
    results = {}
    print(f"Creating {len(FLATTENED_TABLES)} flattened database tables...")
    for table_name, config in FLATTENED_TABLES.items():
        try:
            result = config["schema"]()
            results[table_name] = result
            print(f"✅ Created flattened table: {table_name}")
        except Exception as e:
            results[table_name] = f"Error: {str(e)}"
            print(f"❌ Error creating {table_name}: {e}")
    return results
```

Three separate issues in a 15-line function:

1. **Bare `except Exception`** with no re-raise. If `income_statement` fails to create because MySQL is down or DDL is malformed, the loop keeps going and returns a dict where some values are stringified errors. Downstream code that iterates results likely doesn't check `isinstance(v, str)` — cache reads will then hit `Table doesn't exist` errors much later, far from the root cause.
2. **`print()` for logging** — no stderr/stdout distinction, no log level, no timestamps, no way to silence in tests. Should be `logger.info` / `logger.exception`.
3. **Emoji-decorated status lines** (`✅`, `❌`) will UnicodeEncodeError under Windows `cp1252` consoles (this repo runs on Windows per CLAUDE.md — `.venv_win`).

## Why this matters
Schema-init is the load-bearing step of the cache — if a table doesn't get created, the entire provider is silently degraded. Swallowing the exception means the DB is left in a half-provisioned state with no alarm, and the emoji print will crash the whole init on Windows before the user even sees which table failed.

## Suggested fix
Replace `print` with `logger.info` / `logger.exception`. Convert the loop so that either (a) one exception aborts the whole init and re-raises, or (b) it collects errors but the function returns `(successes, errors)` and callers must check `errors`. Strip the emojis or gate them on `sys.stdout.encoding == 'utf-8'`.

Nearly every table declares `eps DECIMAL(8,6)` and `eps_diluted DECIMAL(8,6)` (first at line 63-64; repeats every table). `DECIMAL(8,6)` has precision 8 and scale 6, so the maximum representable value is `99.999999`. Real-world EPS values regularly exceed this:

```sql
eps DECIMAL(8,6) DEFAULT NULL,
eps_diluted DECIMAL(8,6) DEFAULT NULL,
```

- MSFT TTM EPS ≈ $12 (fits)
- NVDA TTM EPS ≈ $3 (fits)
- BKNG TTM EPS ≈ $180 → **overflow**
- BRK.A TTM EPS ≈ $26,000 → **overflow**
- FCNCA, NVR, AZO, MELI, MKL — all trigger overflow

By default MySQL raises `OUT OF RANGE` errors on insert or, without `STRICT_TRANS_TABLES`, silently truncates to `99.999999`, corrupting the cache. The same bug applies to `beta DECIMAL(8,6)` (some biotech / crypto proxies have betas > 100).

Refuter check: could these columns be intentionally narrow because EPS is stored elsewhere? No — the `data_json` blob is a fallback, not the primary. And `historical_eps`, `financial_ratios`, `key_metrics`, `equity_quote` all query these flat columns. Confirmed real.

## Why this matters
Any pull of a high-EPS ticker either raises a DB error (blocking the cache write) or silently rounds the value to 99.999999 (permanently corrupting historical analysis). Ratios computed downstream (P/E, PEG) will be wildly wrong for the affected symbols. This is the classic 'silent financial data corruption' pattern — hardest kind of bug to detect after the fact.

## Suggested fix
Widen to `DECIMAL(20,6)` (or `DECIMAL(18,4)` if you prefer cent-level precision) for `eps`, `eps_diluted`, and `beta`. Because the DDL is copy-pasted across ~66 tables, factor the money/ratio column templates into a shared string constant so the fix lands in one place. Additionally add `SET SESSION sql_mode = 'STRICT_TRANS_TABLES,NO_ZERO_DATE'` on the connection to make future truncation errors loud.

## Finding

Doubles FMP API consumption on transient FMP failures (rate limits, 5xx). Hides real cache-write bugs from surfacing (e.g., a schema mismatch that always fails `_store_in_cache` becomes a silent 2x cost multiplier). Also masks the original exception type in the re-throw — the user sees the second exception, not the first.

Distinguish failure locations with narrower try blocks: one try around cache read (fall through to FMP fetch on failure), one try around FMP fetch (do not swallow — let it propagate), one try around cache store (log and continue, don't re-fetch). title: [QC-R1][correctness] openbb_platform/providers/fmp_cached/openbb_fmp_cached/models/analyst_estimates.py:396 — Naive datetime.now() written to cached_at — timezone drift between Python and MySQL server

The batch INSERT passes `datetime.now()` (naive, local time) for the `cached_at` column:

But the `cached_at` column is defined `TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` (line 232). MySQL stores TIMESTAMP columns in UTC internally, converting from the session's `time_zone` on write. If any consumer eventually starts using `cached_at` for TTL comparisons (per the previous finding, this is likely once TTL is added), the times will be inconsistent across processes/hosts running in different timezones. Also, since the column has `DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`, explicitly passing `datetime.now()` overrides the sensible default with a less sensible naive value.

Either (a) omit `datetime.now()` from the INSERT tuple and rely on the column DEFAULT (simplest — MySQL fills it consistently); or (b) use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` and ensure the MySQL session runs with `SET time_zone = '+00:00'`. Option (a) is preferable — it removes a value that the DB already generates.

Users get silently truncated result sets that look complete. There's no signal in the return value that the cache was under-filled. ## Finding
```python
for symbol in symbols:
    if not symbol or symbol in seen:
        continue
    seen.add(symbol)
    cleaned.append(symbol)
```

`not symbol` is only False for `None` and `""`. A whitespace-only string like `" "` is truthy in Python and is kept as-is (verified: `bool(" ") is True`). More common in practice: strings with incidental leading/trailing whitespace (`" AAPL"`, `"AAPL "`) survive and are treated as distinct symbols from `"AAPL"`. That defeats the deduplication intent — the caller sees a universe of `["AAPL", " AAPL"]` that any downstream ticker equality check will treat as two symbols. The FMP holdings feed is generally clean today, but caller-supplied constituent lists (via `resolve_universe(cfg, constituents=[...])`) come from arbitrary sources (env vars, CSV imports, user config) where whitespace contamination is routine.

Same class applies to case: `"AAPL"` and `"aapl"` are kept as two symbols. FMP itself is case-consistent, but again the constituent-list path opens that door.

## Why this matters
A `constituent_list` universe like `["AAPL", "MSFT ", " NVDA", ""]` currently resolves to `["AAPL", "MSFT ", " NVDA"]` (3 members, matching `min_members=1`) rather than `["AAPL", "MSFT", "NVDA"]`. The whitespace-contaminated symbols then propagate into `MoverList.movers[i].symbol` and eventually into an Excel `Recommendation` row that no downstream API endpoint will recognize.

## Suggested fix
Strip and dedupe on the normalized form:

```python
for raw in symbols:
    if raw is None:
        continue
    symbol = raw.strip()
    if not symbol or symbol in seen:
        continue
    seen.add(symbol)
    cleaned.append(symbol)
```

Case-normalization (`.upper()`) is a policy call — most US-equity providers are already uppercase, so `.strip()` alone catches ~all real-world contamination; add `.upper()` if you want to defend against user config lower-casing.

## File
`openbb_platform/extensions/techtrade/openbb_techtrade/engine/universe.py:70`

## Finding
`_default_holdings_fetcher` calls `obb.etf.holdings(symbol=etf_symbol, provider="fmp_cached")` with no `date` argument, and `_default_screener_fetcher` calls `obb.equity.screener(sector=fmp_sector, provider="fmp_cached")` — both are point-in-time-today endpoints. `resolve_universe` itself has no `as_of` parameter, so the returned universe is always "today's constituents."

However, downstream call sites bind this universe to a historical session date:

* `openbb_techtrade/engine/movers.py:519` — `_resolve_filter_universe` calls `resolve_universe(config, ...)` to filter movers ranked at `as_of` (movers.py L245–249 goes to some length to bound the OHLCV `end_date` "to avoid look-ahead" — but the *universe itself* it filters against is today's).
* `openbb_techtrade/tuning/sector_ohlcv.py:54` — `universe_for_segment(segment)` in `pool_sector_ohlcv(as_of=...)` seeds tuneta's training pool for a `[as_of - horizon_years, as_of]` window. The pool never includes names that XL* held during that window but no longer holds (delisted, merged, dropped from the sector ETF), and it *does* include names that were added later.

This is textbook survivorship + look-ahead bias for the tune (issue #83) and any historical mover / plan workflow: rankings and tuned hyperparameters are computed against a universe that only losers-who-survived belong to. It systematically over-states realized returns and under-states drawdown in the tuning objective.

## Why this matters
The tuning gate (#82 L2 verdict==robust) is what decides whether a candidate `IndicatorConfig` is persisted. If the candidate is optimised against a survivor-only universe, `verdict` becomes an optimistic estimator of the strategy's real-world edge, and marginal candidates that only look robust because delisted names have been silently dropped get written to `~/.openbb_platform/techtrade_tuned.json`. In short: the L2 gate's floor is silently raised by a data-shape assumption the resolver never advertises.

Same issue exists at *rank* time in `build_mover_list`, though the impact there is smaller (single-session ranking, `as_of` is usually today).

## Suggested fix
Two-part fix, minimum:

1. Add an `as_of: date | None = None` parameter to `resolve_universe` (and thread it through `resolve_all_segments`, `_resolve_filter_universe`, and `universe_for_segment`). Pass it into the fetchers.
2. Have the default fetchers either (a) call an FMP endpoint that supports historical holdings (`/v3/historical/etf/holdings`, or the constituent-history endpoint) when `as_of` is given, or (b) if `as_of` is set and no historical source is wired, raise `NotImplementedError` so the caller has to opt in to today's-holdings semantics explicitly.

At minimum, document the today's-holdings semantics in the module docstring and the `resolve_universe` docstring so downstream callers (especially the tuning bridge) can decide whether they need to snapshot a static `constituent_list` per historical run.

Inline refuter: could this be intentional / already-documented? — The module docstring (L1–18) talks about resolving "live" universes but never says the resolved list reflects the *call* time rather than any `as_of`. `movers.py` explicitly documents avoiding look-ahead on OHLCV (L249), which shows the codebase treats look-ahead as in-scope — the universe gap is inconsistent with that discipline. So it's not a documented design choice; it's an oversight worth surfacing.

title: [QC-R1][correctness] openbb_platform/extensions/techtrade/openbb_techtrade/engine/indicators_technical.py:336 — Bare `except Exception` in technical_panel swallows programming errors alongside runt...
description:
## File
`openbb_platform/extensions/techtrade/openbb_techtrade/engine/indicators_technical.py:336`

## Finding
The technical leg wraps the entire compute pipeline in a broad `except Exception` and, on any failure, silently returns the classic #72 panel with only a WARNING log:

```python
try:
    import pandas_ta_classic  # noqa: F401
    obb = loader()
    records = _to_data_records(df)
    return IndicatorPanel(
        symbol=symbol,
        as_of=as_of,
        trend=_compute_technical_trend(obb, records, config),
        momentum=_compute_technical_momentum(obb, records, config),
        volatility=_compute_technical_volatility(obb, records, config),
        volume=_compute_volume(df, config),
        candles=_compute_candles(df),
    )
except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001 - any technical failure degrades to the deterministic #72 panel
    _logger.warning(
        "technical_panel for %s degraded to the classic #72 builder after an "
        "openbb.technical failure; ...",
        symbol,
        exc_info=True,
    )
    return build_indicator_panel(symbol, as_of, ohlcv_rows, config=config)
```

This catches not just legitimate `obb.technical.*` runtime failures but also programming errors that would otherwise be loud and obvious: a typo in a kwarg name (`fast_k_perid=...`), a stale column-prefix constant after an upstream rename (e.g. pandas_ta renaming `close_MACDh` to `MACDh_12_26_9`), an `AttributeError` from a signature change in openbb_technical, or an incorrect `IndicatorConfig` field access. All of these come back as WARN log lines and a byte-identical classic panel -- consumers see no observable difference.

Compounding the risk, `openbb_technical` is **not installed in this checkout** (per line 54: `"In this checkout the ``technical`` extension is not installed, so this returns ``False`` and the adapter takes the classic fallback path."`). So the try/except block never fires locally. A broken adapter would only be discovered in a production environment that has `openbb_technical` installed, and only if someone reads the warning logs.

## Why this matters
The whole point of this adapter (per docstring lines 4-8) is to source PRD §11 indicators from `obb.technical.*` when available for parity with the first-party extension. If a maintenance change to this file breaks the technical leg, the fallback silently produces the classic panel -- which is *close but not identical*, per the design (technical's `mamode`/`scalar` defaults were chosen to align, but computation ordering, dropna semantics, and column selection may diverge). Users think they're getting technical-sourced values; they're actually getting classic-sourced values. This is the exact 'silent defaults mask real config' pattern flagged in the sweep context: the parity contract is claimed but never enforced.

## Suggested fix
Narrow the except and/or add a counter/metric so silent degradation is observable:

1. **Narrow the except** to the failure classes actually expected from openbb_technical (`ImportError` for missing extension; `AttributeError` for signature mismatch; `KeyError` for missing columns; `ValueError` for insufficient bars). Let `TypeError` (typos in kwargs) and other programming errors propagate:
   ```python
   except (ImportError, AttributeError, KeyError, ValueError):
       _logger.warning(...)
       return build_indicator_panel(...)
   ```
2. **Add a module-level counter** (or emit a distinct log field) so operators can see how often the technical leg degrades:
   ```python
   _technical_degradations = 0  # module-level
   ...
   _technical_degradations += 1
   _logger.warning("... (degradations=%d)", symbol, _technical_degradations, exc_info=True)
   ```
3. **Add a test** that verifies the technical leg actually populates covered keys with technical-sourced values (not the classic fallback silently masquerading). The existing `test_technical_leg_populates_all_covered_keys` uses a fake obb that runs classic pandas_ta_classic under the hood, so classic-vs-technical parity is tested but never technical-vs-broken-technical detection.

The pure core `build_indicator_panel` implements the #83 L9 auto-load exclusively behind an `if config is None:` branch (line 540) that consults `lookup_tuned_for_symbol(symbol)` on `~/.openbb_platform/techtrade_tuned.json`. Because the wrapper's default value is `DEFAULT_CONFIG` (a real `IndicatorConfig` instance, not `None`), that branch NEVER fires for any caller that goes through the live wrapper -- even after tuning has produced a robust per-sector config on disk. The type annotation `IndicatorConfig` (not `IndicatorConfig | None`) additionally forbids callers from opting in by passing `config=None`, so mypy rejects the only workaround.

L9 is the mechanism by which sector-tuned indicator periods (produced by the tuning pipeline) actually reach production panel builds. With this bug, the on-disk `techtrade_tuned.json` file has zero effect on the live/integration path -- every symbol silently gets `DEFAULT_CONFIG` (PRD §11 vanilla).     calendar: str = "XNYS",


And update the wrapper's docstring (lines 634-635) to point to `build_indicator_panel`'s config description so the L9 auto-load behaviour is discoverable from the live-facing entry point. Add a regression test that (a) writes a tuned config for a segment via `write_tuned`, (b) calls `build_panel_for_symbol` with an injected fake fetcher for a symbol in that segment, and (c) asserts the resulting panel reflects the tuned periods (not `DEFAULT_CONFIG`).

title: [QC-R1][correctness] openbb_platform/extensions/techtrade/openbb_techtrade/execution/broker.py:203 — PaperBroker fills stop orders AT the stop level even on gap-through bars, understating loss
description:
## File
`openbb_platform/extensions/techtrade/openbb_techtrade/execution/broker.py:203`

## Finding
`_reference_price` for a stop order returns the stop level itself whenever the bar touches it intrabar:

```python
if order.order_type == "stop":
    level = order.stop_price
    if level is None:
        return None
    high, low = _dec(_get(bar, "high")), _dec(_get(bar, "low"))
    triggered = high >= level if is_buy else low <= level
    return level if triggered else None
```

This is fine when the bar trades DOWN through the stop intrabar (real-world fill is very close to the stop level). But when the market **gaps through** the stop at open -- e.g., long entry at 121.40 with `stop_price=117.60`, next-day bar opens at 114.00 (overnight gap-down) -- the current code still fills at `117.60 - 5bps = 117.5412`, whereas the real-market fill would be near the open at ~114.00. That's a $3.54/share overstatement of the exit price, i.e., a materially *understated* loss.

The module docstring at line 20 markets the tie-break as "**conservative stop-wins**" and highlights choosing "the worse path" -- but this gap-through behavior is the *opposite* of conservative. It systematically flatters strategies whose stops get gapped through (news-driven names, small-caps, illiquid periods).

## Why this matters
This is a real risk in a backtesting/paper-trading tool. The whole point of the paper broker is to give traders an honest read on strategy performance before committing capital. Systematically flattering the loss side biases the composite score in `Recommendation`, biases the tearsheet metrics, and could push a strategy across a promote/publish threshold that a live broker's actual gap fill would fail. Popular open-source backtesters (backtesting.py, vectorbt) handle this by using `fill_price = min(open, stop)` for long stops (max for short stops). Users familiar with those tools will assume the same guarantee here.

## Suggested fix
For a long stop: `fill_price = min(_dec(_get(bar, "open")), level)` before slippage. For a short stop: `max(open, level)`. Add a unit test with a gap-down bar (open=114, low=113, stop=117.60) and assert the fill lands at 114 - slip, not 117.60 - slip. If the current behavior is intentional for v1 (a documented simplification), add a `Notes` section to the class docstring calling it out explicitly so users don't discover it when a real trade blows their model.

Any validation whose `plan.as_of` lands on a leap day (Feb 29 of 2016/2020/2024/2028…) silently loses one day of history at the *start* of every fold window vs. the same run anchored one session earlier or later. That's a systematic, silent, direction-biased shortening of the training window on a small but non-empty subset of runs — exactly the shape of bug the validation gate is meant to catch elsewhere.

## Suggested fix
Roll back to Feb 28 to match convention and maximize fold length: `return date(as_of.year - horizon_years, 2, 28)`. Or replace the manual arithmetic with `pd.Timestamp(as_of) - pd.DateOffset(years=horizon_years)` / `as_of + relativedelta(years=-horizon_years)`, both of which clamp to Feb 28 automatically. Whichever direction is chosen, spell it out in the docstring so callers know the window can be truncated by one day on leap-day anchors.

title: [QC-R1][correctness] openbb_platform/extensions/techtrade/openbb_techtrade/validation/confluence_strategy.py:157 — isinstance(now, date) is always True for pd.Timestamp — normalization branch is de...
description:
## File
`openbb_platform/extensions/techtrade/openbb_techtrade/validation/confluence_strategy.py:157`

## Finding
```python
now = data.now
# ``data.now`` is a pd.Timestamp; the panel builder takes a date.
as_of_date: date = pd.Timestamp(now).date() if not isinstance(now, date) else now
```

`pd.Timestamp` inherits from `datetime.datetime`, which inherits from `datetime.date`. So `isinstance(pd.Timestamp(...), date)` returns True, and the ternary always takes the `else` branch: `as_of_date = now`. The Timestamp is passed through unchanged; the `pd.Timestamp(now).date()` conversion is unreachable for the exact case (`data.now` is a `pd.Timestamp`) the comment says it exists to handle.

Refuter note: pydantic v2 coerces the passed-through Timestamp when it lands on `IndicatorPanel.as_of: date`, so the live blast radius is small (log formatting is the only observable). But the code is still misleading: `as_of_date` is annotated `date`, isn't one, and the guard's intent isn't achieved.

## Why this matters
Today the impact is limited to log-formatting drift (Timestamp formats as `'2020-01-01 00:00:00'`, plain date as `'2020-01-01'`) because pydantic v2's lax coercion downstream saves the model field. But the annotation lies to readers, the guard is dead code that will silently keep being dead as protocols change, and any future stricter downstream check (e.g. `type(x) is date`) will regress silently on every validation run.

## Suggested fix
Drop the broken ternary and always normalize: `as_of_date: date = pd.Timestamp(now).date()` — this works whether `now` is a Timestamp, `datetime`, or plain `date` (all accepted by the `pd.Timestamp` constructor, and `.date()` returns a plain `date`). Or, if avoiding the round-trip on already-plain dates matters, use exact-type discrimination: `as_of_date = now if type(now) is date else pd.Timestamp(now).date()`.

title: [QC-R1][correctness] openbb_platform/extensions/techtrade/openbb_techtrade/tuning/tuneta_adapter.py:48 — KNOB_TABLE MACD ranges allow degenerate configs where macd_fast >= macd_slow
description:
## File
`openbb_platform/extensions/techtrade/openbb_techtrade/tuning/tuneta_adapter.py:48`

## Finding
The MACD knobs share a boundary and are sampled by tuneta independently:

```python
KNOB_TABLE: tuple[tuple[str, str, tuple[int, int]], ...] = (
    ("macd_fast",    "tta.MACD", (8, 20)),
    ("macd_slow",    "tta.MACD", (20, 40)),
    ("macd_signal",  "tta.MACD", (5, 15)),
    ...
)
```

tuneta samples each range as an independent parameter. A trial with `macd_fast=20` and `macd_slow=20` — or the more general `macd_fast >= macd_slow` — produces a degenerate MACD (the fast-EMA is not faster than the slow-EMA, so the MACD line is zero-mean or negative). `parse_tuned_columns` will faithfully bind these values into IndicatorConfig without validation, and `write_tuned` will persist them if the verdict happens to come back 'robust' by chance.

Same concern (weaker) applies to the EMA overlap at period 30 — see docstring at line 128 acknowledging '30 binds to ema_fast' — which means tuneta may burn trials sampling a slow-EMA period of 30 that silently binds to the fast slot, so the second knob is effectively no-op for that trial.

## Why this matters
Degenerate MACD configs waste tuneta trials on hyperparameter values that produce useless indicators. Worse, the fit objective (forward-return correlation) is measured against these bad indicators; a trial that scores well by noise gets promoted. The gate at `verdict == 'robust'` may catch obviously bad results, but subtle degradation from a few degenerate trials contaminates the optuna search history and slows convergence.

## Suggested fix
Two-part fix:
1. Tighten KNOB_TABLE ranges to be disjoint and monotonic: `macd_fast (8, 19)`, `macd_slow (21, 40)`, `ema_fast (10, 29)`, `ema_slow (31, 80)`.
2. Add a post-parse validation in `parse_tuned_columns` (or `fit_segment`) that rejects and re-samples any trial where `macd_fast >= macd_slow` OR `ema_fast >= ema_slow`. If re-sampling is not supported by tuneta, log a WARNING and treat the trial as pruned.
Bonus: add a unit test in `test_tuneta_adapter.py` that feeds `parse_tuned_columns` a synthetic column set with `fastperiod_20_slowperiod_20` and asserts the invariant.

## Finding
`write_tuned` begins by reading the existing file to merge the new segment in:

```python
current = read_tuned() or {"schema_version": SCHEMA_VERSION, "segments": {}}

    "meta": meta,
```

`read_tuned()` returns `None` in FOUR distinct scenarios (from `_read_tuned_cached`):
1. File not found — safe, nothing to wipe.
2. JSON parse failure (partial write from a prior crash, hand-edit typo, encoding corruption) — logs a WARNING but returns None.
3. Schema version mismatch — logs a WARNING but returns None.
4. Top-level JSON is not an object — logs a WARNING but returns None.

A single corrupt-file event or schema-version bump silently discards the user's entire tuning history. Re-tuning is expensive (`trials=100` optuna trials × 11 sectors × ~minutes each). 1. Backup-and-restart: before overwrite, copy the un-parseable file to `<TUNED_PATH>.corrupt.<timestamp>` so nothing is lost.
2. Fail-loud: `write_tuned` raises when the existing file exists but returns None, with the log context, so the user consciously decides whether to nuke it.
3. Schema migration: for schema version mismatches specifically, attempt a migration path rather than a silent wipe.
At minimum, log at ERROR (not WARNING) when write_tuned is about to replace a non-empty but unreadable file.

description:
## File
`openbb_platform/extensions/techtrade/openbb_techtrade/tuning/tune_router.py:126`

## Finding
The public `tune()` router command accepts user-controlled tuning knobs with no bounds or schema checks:

```python
async def tune(
    segment: str,
    *,
    ...
    trials: int = 100,
    early_stop: int = 20,
    method: str = "wfo",
    thresholds: dict[str, float] | None = None,
    provider: str | None = None,
) -> OBBject:
```

- `trials`: no upper bound. `trials=10**6` runs 1M optuna trials — hours-to-days on 4 workers, no timeout. `trials=0` or `trials=-1` reach `fit_segment` before failing with a confusing tuneta error.
- `early_stop`: no bound. `early_stop > trials` silently disables early stopping.
- `thresholds`: arbitrary dict, no schema. Unknown keys are silently ignored by `validate_plan` (or worse, override intended defaults).
- `method`: string not restricted to the {'wfo', ...} set that validate_plan actually supports.

## Why this matters
A CLI user with a fat-finger error (`trials=1000` when they meant `100`) burns 10× the CPU without a warning. A programmatic caller passing `thresholds={'pbo_ok': 0.5}` when the real key is `pbo` gets a silent no-op — the tune runs at default thresholds and the caller thinks their gate is active. Missing validation on user hyperparameter grids is a common failure pattern in tuning wrappers (Ralph flagged this pattern for the sweep).

## Suggested fix
Add a pre-flight validation block at the top of `tune()` (before `_require_tuneta()`):
```python

    raise ValueError(f"trials must be in [1, 10000], got {trials}")
if not 1 <= early_stop <= trials:
    raise ValueError(f"early_stop must be in [1, trials], got {early_stop}")
if method not in {"wfo", "cpcv"}:  # or import the canonical set
    raise ValueError(f"method {method!r} not in {{'wfo','cpcv'}}")
if thresholds is not None:
    _allowed = {"pbo", "deflated_sharpe", "oos_sharpe"}
    _bad = set(thresholds) - _allowed
    if _bad:
        raise ValueError(f"unknown thresholds keys: {sorted(_bad)}; allowed: {sorted(_allowed)}")
```

description:
## File
`openbb_platform/extensions/techtrade/openbb_techtrade/strategies/presets.py:121`

## Finding
The module docstring explicitly warns that volume overrides are **inert end-to-end**:

> "A preset (or override) that set a different ``volume`` would therefore be **inert end-to-end** -- ignored by both the multiplier and the vote stamping (which both hardcode ``DEFAULT_WEIGHTS.volume``) -- so every preset pins ``volume = 0.15`` to keep its declared weights honest"

But `resolve_preset` still *accepts* volume overrides, only bounds-checking:

```python

    raise ValueError(f"volume must be in [0, 1], got {merged.volume}.")
```

So `resolve_preset("trend_follow", {"volume": 0.5})` returns `ConfluenceWeights(..., volume=0.5)` with no error. Downstream, `volume_confirmation` hardcodes `DEFAULT_WEIGHTS.volume` (0.15) — the caller's 0.5 is silently discarded. The user believes they configured volume=0.5; the engine runs with 0.15.

The function-level docstring mentions the [0,1] rule but not the inertness. Only readers of the *module* docstring learn that any non-0.15 override is a no-op.

## Why this matters
This is the exact 'silent defaults mask real config' pattern flagged in the sweep context. A caller who overrides volume to tune their strategy gets zero effect but zero warning — their tuning experiments will show the same output every time, and they will spend real time debugging why volume tuning does nothing before eventually finding the module docstring. Worse, the API pretends configurability where none exists: the validator's [0,1] check *implies* the range matters, but the range only matters for a value that is never used.

1. **Reject non-fixed volume overrides explicitly** (recommended — matches the doc's 'presets pin volume=0.15 to keep declared weights honest' intent):
   ```python

       raise ValueError(
           f"volume is engine-fixed at {FIXED_VOLUME} (volume_confirmation hardcodes "
           f"DEFAULT_WEIGHTS.volume); overrides other than {FIXED_VOLUME} are silently "
           f"ignored downstream. Remove the override or change volume_confirmation."
       )
   ```
2. **Emit a `UserWarning`** when a non-FIXED_VOLUME override is passed (less surprising but weaker — warnings are easy to miss).

Either way, mirror the resolution to the function-level docstring's `Raises:` (or `Warns:`) section so callers reading only that docstring see it.
